title: Manage organic certification and internal control systems

lessons.title: Managing the certification process
lessons.html:
The manager's role

Managing organic certification means taking responsibility for compliance, documentation, relationships with the certification body and buyers, and continuous improvement. Whether for a single farm or a producer group, the manager makes sure the operation can prove at any time that it meets the standard.

Choosing the standard and certifier

  • Identify target markets; each may require a specific standard (for example the EU, US or other national organic regulations, or local and participatory schemes).
  • Select an accredited or recognised certification body that can certify to the required standards.
  • Understand costs: application, inspection, certification fees, lab testing and internal costs.

Preparing the operation

  1. Organic management plan (OMP): describes the farm, fields, crops and livestock, inputs, soil fertility plan, pest and disease management, contamination prevention, buffer zones, water sources, harvesting, storage, processing and record systems.
  2. Conversion: register land and begin the conversion period set by the standard; plan cash flow, since products may not carry organic premiums during conversion.
  3. Input approval: check every input (fertilisers, compost ingredients, seed, pest control products, cleaning agents, feed, vet treatments) against the standard; keep proof of approval.
  4. Seed and planting material: organic seed where available; documented derogations where allowed.
  5. Parallel production controls: if conventional and organic production coexist, separate equipment, storage and records rigorously.

Inspection and certification cycle

  • Annual announced inspection: documents, fields, stores, processing, interviews and a traceability or mass balance check (inputs and harvest versus sales).
  • Possible unannounced inspections and residue sampling.
  • Non-conformities issued with deadlines for corrective action.
  • Certificate issued or renewed, specifying products and scope.

Sanctions for serious breaches can include loss of certification for products or fields, so the manager must respond to findings promptly.

lessons.title: Running an internal control system
lessons.html:
ICS management structure

For group certification, the certification body evaluates the effectiveness of the group's internal control system and re-inspects a sample of members. The ICS manager is responsible for the system as a whole.

FunctionResponsibility
ICS managerOverall coordination, documentation, liaison with certifier
Internal inspectorsInspect every member at least annually; should not inspect their own farms or close relatives
Approval committeeDecides approval, conditions or sanctions for each member based on inspection reports
Field officersAdvise and train farmers
Buying and warehouse staffBuy only from approved members, check volumes, keep products separate

Separating advice from inspection where possible reduces conflicts of interest.

Core ICS documents

  • Internal standard in local language
  • Member list with farm details, status (conversion or certified), estimated yields
  • Signed member agreements
  • Farm maps and field histories
  • Inspection checklists and reports
  • Approval committee decisions and sanctions register
  • Training records
  • Purchase records reconciled against yield estimates
  • Risk assessment identifying high-risk members or areas, such as farms bordering conventional sprayed crops

Risk-based control

Focus additional inspections, residue testing and training on high-risk members: new members, members with previous non-conformities, farms with parallel production, those next to conventional farms, or deliveries above estimated yield.

Managing non-compliance

Apply a clear, published sanctions catalogue consistently, from warnings to suspension and exclusion. Record all cases and follow up. Inform the certification body as required.

Continuous improvement

  • Hold annual internal reviews of the ICS.
  • Analyse inspection findings for common problems and target training.
  • Update the internal standard when external standards change.
  • Communicate regularly with members about prices, premiums and rules.

Key points

  • Choose standards and certifiers based on target markets.
  • An organic management plan and input approvals are the foundation of compliance.
  • Annual inspections include document review and mass balance checks.
  • An ICS needs independent internal inspectors, an approval committee and sanctions.
  • Use risk-based controls and continuous review to protect the group certificate.
